markets.title: Will the US or EU mandate government-run or accredited pre-deployment safety evals for frontier AI models by 2028?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2028, either (a) the US enacts a federal statute or binding federal agency rule (e.g., via Commerce/CAISI, DoD, or a newly authorized federal AI agency) or (b) the EU adopts a binding Regulation, Directive, or EU AI Office Implementing Act amending or extending the EU AI Act, that legally prohibits commercial release or external deployment of frontier AI models above a specified training-compute (e.g., >=10^26 FLOP) or dangerous-capability threshold (CBRN, offensive cyber, or autonomy) until the model completes pre-deployment safety evaluations or red-teaming conducted by a government institute (such as US CAISI or the EU AI Office) or an accredited independent third-party evaluator (such as METR or Apollo). Excludes voluntary commitments, US state-only laws (e.g., CA SB 53), and the pre-existing 2024 EU AI Act Article 55 self-assessment, voluntary GPAI Code of Practice, and post-hoc Article 91 RFIs unless upgraded to mandatory pre-deployment external/government evaluation clearance.

markets.title: Will the US enact tighter China AI chip export controls beyond the Nov 2026 BIS baseline by 2028?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2028, the US enacts a binding federal statute (e.g., codifying the MATCH Act, GAIN AI Act, or statutory China accelerator bans) or Commerce/BIS publishes an effective Final or Interim Final Rule in the Federal Register that materially tightens AI compute export controls on China/Country Group D:5 relative to the November 19, 2026 BIS baseline via at least one of: (1) revoking the January 2026 case-by-case review pathway and restoring a formal presumption of denial for H200-class or lower-threshold ECCN 3A090 accelerators to China/Macau; (2) cutting the ECCN 3A090 Total Processing Performance (TPP) export ceiling for China by >=25% or lowering the November 19, 2026 remote-access cloud license threshold below 12 million aggregate TPP; or (3) expanding binding extraterritorial Foreign Direct Product Rule controls on advanced packaging, HBM3E/HBM4, or sub-14nm DUV lithography servicing to Chinese fabs. Resolves NO if controls remain at or are relaxed below the November 19, 2026 baseline.

markets.title: Will the US enact a federal AI lab whistleblower protection and frontier incident reporting law by 2028?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2028, an Act of Congress is signed into US federal law (such as the AI Whistleblower Protection Act or a broader federal AI safety statute) that contains BOTH: (1) explicit federal anti-retaliation protections and NDA carve-outs shielding current or former employees and contractors of frontier AI developers who report catastrophic AI safety, alignment, or weight-security risks to federal authorities or Congress; AND (2) mandatory federal incident-reporting obligations requiring covered frontier AI developers (defined by compute, capability, or revenue thresholds) to notify a designated federal agency (e.g., DHS/CISA, Commerce/CAISI, or a federal AI oversight office) within a statutory deadline upon discovering qualifying severe model-weight exfiltrations, cyber breaches, or autonomous loss-of-control / critical safety incidents. State-only statutes (e.g., CA SB 53) and non-binding executive policies do not qualify.

markets.title: Will the US enact a federal frontier-model licensing or compute-threshold regulatory statute by 2029?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2029, an Act of Congress is signed into US federal law establishing a binding federal licensing, pre-training registration-and-authorization, or statutory compute-threshold regulatory regime governing frontier AI models (e.g., models exceeding an explicit training-compute threshold such as >=10^26 or >=10^27 FLOP, cluster power threshold, or frontier capability tier), empowering a federal agency to enforce binding safety/security standards, audit labs, and deny, suspend, or revoke authorization to train or deploy non-compliant frontier models. Excludes purely voluntary NIST frameworks, standalone state-preemption moratoriums lacking substantive federal frontier standards, and export-control rules applying solely to foreign adversaries.

markets.title: Will the US or EU enact statutory strict liability or mandatory insurance for autonomous AI agents by 2029?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2029, either (a) the US enacts a federal statute or (b) the EU adopts a new binding Regulation or Directive published in the Official Journal specifically establishing either: (1) a statutory strict-liability regime imposing non-waivable civil liability on frontier model developers or commercial deployers for material financial, cyber, or physical harm caused by autonomous AI agents operating without per-action human approval; OR (2) a mandatory third-party liability insurance, financial-responsibility bond, or Price-Anderson-style pooled catastrophe indemnity fund required as a legal condition to deploy frontier/high-autonomy AI agents. Explicitly excludes the pre-existing 2024 EU Product Liability Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/2853) as enacted prior to November 2026 unless newly amended or supplemented with autonomous-agent strict-liability or mandatory-insurance rules.

markets.title: Will the US enact a federal ban or export-style licensing restriction on releasing frontier open-weight models by 2030?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2030, the US enacts a federal statute or binding federal regulation (e.g., under EAR/BIS, ITAR, or a federal AI regulatory statute) that takes legal effect and prohibits, or requires prior federal government license/authorization before, US persons or entities publicly releasing the model weights of a frontier AI model above a defined compute threshold (e.g., >=10^26 or >=10^27 FLOP) or dangerous-capability threshold (CBRN, offensive cyber zero-day exploitation, or autonomous replication). Voluntary lab decisions not to release weights, non-binding guidance, or rules permanently enjoined before taking effect do not qualify.

markets.title: Will the US and China sign a bilateral AI safety or frontier compute-monitoring agreement by 2030?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2030, the governments of the United States and the People's Republic of China formally sign a bilateral written agreement, executive accord, or treaty (beyond non-binding Track 2 dialogues or generic summit communiques) establishing concrete operational commitments in at least one of: (1) mutual notification, verification, or monitoring of frontier AI training clusters/runs above a defined compute threshold; (2) verifiable bilateral red lines and crisis communication protocols governing autonomous AI in nuclear command-and-control, critical-infrastructure cyber offense, or bioweapons; or (3) mutual or jointly audited third-party safety evaluation and critical-incident disclosure protocols for frontier AI labs. Formal Senate treaty ratification is not required if signed as an operational government-to-government executive agreement.

markets.title: Will the US mandate hardware-enforced location tracking or on-chip compute governance on frontier AI accelerators by 2030?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2030, the US enacts a federal statute (such as the Chip Security Act, H.R. 3447 / S. 1705, or successor legislation) or Commerce/BIS issues an effective binding rule requiring manufacturers of export-controlled frontier AI accelerators (ECCN 3A090 or successor datacenter GPU/TPU/ASIC classifications) to integrate hardware- or firmware-enforced governance mechanisms into newly shipped chips — specifically including cryptographic location verification (e.g., delay-based geolocation or signed location attestation), hardware-enforced cluster-size/telemetry attestation, or remote licensing/disablement capability. Paper end-user attestations or software-only cloud KYC rules (such as the Nov 2026 BIS Remote Access IFR) without mandated on-chip/firmware security mechanisms do not qualify.

markets.title: Will a >=1 GW majority government-owned sovereign AI compute cluster outside the US and China be operational by 2030?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, by December 31, 2030, at least one sovereign AI compute cluster or national/supranational public compute reserve located outside the United States and China (including Hong Kong and Macau) reaches verified operational status with >=1.0 GW (1,000 MW) of energized IT/AI-compute load (at a single campus or within one integrated national/EU-level public compute reserve such as an EU AI Gigafactory/EuroHPC facility, UAE sovereign-controlled 1 GW+ campus once fully energized, Saudi HUMAIN sovereign cluster, or UK national compute reserve), where >=50% equity ownership or direct operational/allocation control is held by a national government, sovereign wealth fund, or intergovernmental public body. Announced plans, power-permit filings, or sub-1 GW initial phases (such as the 200 MW 2026 Phase 1 of Stargate UAE) do not qualify until >=1.0 GW of active AI compute load is operational.

markets.title: Will the US launch a >=$50B government-directed frontier AI mega-project or nationalize a frontier AI lab by 2031?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2031, the US federal government either: (1) enacts federal appropriations or binding federal fiscal commitments totaling >=$50 billion (nominal USD via direct funding, DOE/DoD contracts, or federally backed consortium equity/loans) establishing a single US government-directed frontier AI development mega-project or public-private national compute consortium ('AI Manhattan Project') with direct federal governance and security authority over training runs and model weights; OR (2) exercises statutory authority (e.g., Defense Production Act compulsion, eminent domain, or federal receivership/nationalization legislation) to assume direct operational control or majority federal ownership of a US frontier AI lab (such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind US, or xAI). Privately financed hyperscaler projects endorsed rhetorically by the White House without >=$50B in binding federal financing or direct federal operational command do not qualify.

markets.title: Will the US or G7 enact an emergency >=90-day moratorium on frontier AI training following a safety or capability scare by 2031?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, between November 24, 2026 and December 31, 2031, the US federal government (via statute, legally enforceable executive order, or binding federal agency order) OR a coordinated binding directive of at least four G7 governments (including the US) enforces a temporary halt lasting at least 90 consecutive calendar days prohibiting initiation or continuation of frontier AI training runs above a specified compute or capability threshold, explicitly citing safety, misalignment, loss-of-control, weight-security, or catastrophic capability risks. Voluntary pauses by individual labs, pauses lifted before 90 consecutive days, or state/local datacenter zoning moratoriums targeting electricity or water usage do not qualify; carve-outs for government-supervised safety/alignment research remain compatible with a YES resolution.

markets.title: Will an IAEA-style international AI inspection agency with hardware-verified compute audits be established by treaty by 2033?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, by December 31, 2033, a legally binding multilateral treaty or international charter enters into force (ratified by at least 10 states, including at least two of the United States, China, and the European Union/EU member states) establishing a permanent intergovernmental AI inspection and verification organization (analogous to the IAEA or OPCW) vested with legal authority to conduct on-site datacenter inspections OR hardware-verified compute audits (verifying accelerator inventories, cryptographic chip telemetry, power consumption, or frontier training-run compliance) within signatory jurisdictions. Advisory UN panels, voluntary AI Safety Institute networks, and non-binding international summit declarations without binding inspection/audit authority do not qualify.

markets.title: Will the US and China both ratify a binding global compute-cap or frontier AI training ceiling treaty by 2035?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, by December 31, 2035, BOTH the United States (via Senate treaty ratification or congressional-executive agreement enacted into federal statute) and the People's Republic of China (via ratification by the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress) have formally ratified and brought into force a legally binding international treaty imposing verifiable upper limits (hard compute caps, moratoria, or treaty-authorized licensing ceilings) on frontier AI training FLOPs, unapproved frontier cluster aggregation, or unauthorized superhuman capability training runs, backed by mutual or independent verification provisions. Non-binding executive pledges, unilateral domestic ceilings, or treaties ratified by only one of the two powers do not qualify.

markets.title: Will major powers ratify a global post-AGI superintelligence governance or compute-monopoly charter by 2040?
markets.description: Resolves YES if, by December 31, 2040, major powers — including at least the United States, China (or their successor sovereign entities), and either the European Union or at least two additional UN Security Council / G7 / G20 major economies — formally ratify and bring into force a binding global civilizational governance treaty or supranational charter governing post-AGI / superintelligent AI systems, featuring at least one of: (1) consolidating frontier/superintelligent compute infrastructure under a treaty-governed international consortium or licensed global compute monopoly; (2) establishing binding supranational enforcement authority over alignment standards, sovereign AI deployment, and prevention of unauthorized recursive self-improvement worldwide; or (3) establishing a treaty-mandated global post-AGI sovereign compute-allocation or benefit-sharing compact backed by verified global chip-supply and datacenter controls. Regional pacts excluding either the US or China, or symbolic UN declarations without binding enforcement over frontier compute or superintelligent systems, do not qualify.
